analysis.one_liner: Requires the IRS to offer tax forms pre-filled with information it already has on file.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury Department to let taxpayers download their 1040 forms pre-filled with wage, withholding, and income data the government already collects from employers and banks. Taxpayers would check the numbers, add anything missing, and file. It also moved the deadline for employers and banks to send in those records from spring to January 31, so the pre-filled data would be ready sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of taxpayers who now spend hours — or pay preparers — to retype information the IRS already has. Wage earners with simple returns would benefit most, since their wages and withholding are fully reported to the government each year.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs Treasury to provide a secure download of pre-populated 1040, 1040A, and 1040EZ forms, both printable and in a format tax software can import, starting with the 2015 tax year [S2] [S3].

The pre-filled forms would use wage and self-employment income data the Social Security Administration already collects, with employers required to report wages by January 31 instead of later in the spring, so the data would be available when filing season starts [S2] [S3].
Taxpayers keep full responsibility for accuracy and must acknowledge before downloading that the pre-filled information needs verification, addressing the risk of filing from incomplete data [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Paid tax preparation and tax software companies, which earn fees for helping people enter information the government already holds. Employers and banks also face an earlier reporting deadline, and the IRS would bear the cost of building and securing the download system.

drawbacks.text: The pre-filled form would only contain what was reported to the government, so people with income not reported on information returns — or with errors in employer filings — could still file inaccurate returns; the bill responds by requiring a verification acknowledgment but not by verifying anything [S3].

Employers and financial institutions would have to prepare W-2s, 1099s, and similar forms a full two months earlier, with no extension allowed, a real compliance cost passed through to businesses of every size [S3].

Building and securing a nationwide download system would be a significant new IRS responsibility, and critics of IRS-provided filing data have raised privacy and accuracy concerns about government handling of taxpayer data.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most wage earners the benefit is real and straightforward: less time and less money spent re-entering data the IRS already has. The main costs — earlier employer reporting and an IRS build-out — are modest relative to the time saved by tens of millions of filers each year. The bill is careful, requiring verification and leaving taxpayers responsible, but it stops short of return-free filing, so taxpayers with complex situations get less benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Foster introduced the Autofill Act on April 13, 2015, joined by Reps. Quigley and Doggett [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is where any tax bill must go, and no further action was recorded before the 114th Congress ended [S5].
The committee never held a markup or scheduled a vote, so the bill never reached the House floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Paid tax preparation and software companies, which continue to charge taxpayers to compile data the government already possesses. No taxpayer gained the pre-filled forms the bill promised.

for.name: Rep. Bill Foster
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Autofill Act directing Treasury to provide pre-populated tax forms

for.name: Reps. Mike Quigley and Lloyd Doggett

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill and never scheduled it for a floor vote

against.name: Tax preparation and tax software industry
against.what_they_did: Has a long, well-documented history of lobbying against government-provided pre-filled and return-free filing, the service this bill would begin to supply

sides.party_line_note: The bill had three Democratic sponsors and never advanced far enough for any vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software companies
industries.note: Pre-filled government forms would cut into the core value paid preparers and software companies sell: transferring data from W-2s and 1099s into a return. Their interest in keeping that service paid runs against taxpayers who would get the same data free.

They would have had to file wage and income information returns by January 31 with no extension, roughly two months earlier than before. The cost is real but the earlier data is what makes pre-filled forms possible for workers.
